title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Ellen Park
body:
Summary

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference for Redwood Inference: architecture overview, kernel selection and scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and performance-oriented ML infrastructure owners.

Scope

- Production inference serving runtime (hosted + dedicated + private)
- Kernel selection and scheduling policies that affect latency, throughput, and cost
- Profiling and benchmarking playbooks for regressions and capacity planning
- Runbooks and incident response for common runtime failures
- Release notes summary for the latest stable runtime release

Architecture overview (short)

The serving runtime is composed of the following logical subsystems:

1) API & Request Layer
- Ingress, auth, rate limiting, and request shaping.
- Translates Redwood API calls into runtime jobs.

2) Router & Smart Routing
- Routes requests by policy (latency SLO, cost tier, region) and selects a compatible model variant.

3) Batcher / Scheduler
- Continuous batching front-end that aggregates requests into micro-batches.
- Scheduling policies select kernels and dispatch units to GPU executors.

4) KV Cache & Prefix Cache
- Sharded in-memory KV cache for transformer KV states (per-tenant / per-route).
- Cache lookup and warm-path optimization to bypass compute when possible.

5) Executor / Kernel Runtime
- GPU-optimized operators (attention, matmul variants, rotary embeddings, quantized kernels).
- Kernel selection layer chooses kernels by model arch, sequence length, hardware capability.

6) Autoscaler & Capacity Manager
- Manages GPU pools, burst capacity, and fallback routing to compatible model variants.

- Router: eng-platform (owner: Mateo Rodrigues)
- Batcher & Scheduler: eng-serving-runtime (owner: Ellen Park)
- Executor & Kernel selection: eng-serving-runtime (owner: Lucas Becker)

- Autoscaler: eng-sre (owner: Ravi Singh)

Kernel selection and scheduling policies (detailed)

Design goals:
- Meet 99th-percentile latency SLOs for interactive routes (typically 150-400ms depending on plan)
- Maximize GPU utilization for throughput-oriented routes while preserving latency targets
- Prefer lower-cost quantized kernels where quality regression is acceptable

Scheduling inputs:
- Model signature: architecture, parameter dtype, supported kernels
- Request profile: batchable / streaming, max output length, temperature/top_p
- Sequence length distribution history (sliding 24h histogram)
- Hardware capabilities: compute SMs, GPU memory, ECC flags, compute capability
- SLO tier: interactive, batched, bulk

Policy examples:
1) Latency-first (interactive)
- Kernel choice: lowest-latency kernel compatible with dtype (FP16/FP32 preferred over int8 if int8 causes regressions)
- Scheduling: preemptive micro-batching with max batch size = 8, max waiting window = 8ms
- Replica choice: use low-congestion GPU pool and warm KV-cache shard

2) Throughput-first (batching)
- Kernel choice: high-throughput vectorized kernels (tensor cores, fused-attention) possibly quantized int8
- Scheduling: accumulate up to max_batch = 128 or until 50ms window elapses
- Autoscale: use reserved dedicated capacity pool and enable packing across tenants with compatible SLOs

3) Cost-constrained (best-effort)
- Kernel choice: int8/4-bit quantized kernels with fallback to higher precision on quality regression
- Scheduling: larger batch targets, opportunistic routing to spot capacity

Kernel selection algorithm (runtime summary)
- Step 1: filter kernels by model compatibility (dtype, operator support)
- Step 2: score kernels by expected latency at target sequence length (profiling table) and measured quality delta (from model onboarding)
- Step 3: apply policy weighting (latency vs cost vs quality) and select top candidate
- Step 4: if candidate is saturated, fallback to next-best compatible kernel or route to different pool

Profiling playbook (how to reproduce and triage perf regressions)

Purpose: Provide deterministic steps to profile regressions, collect artifacts, and produce actionable fixes.

Before you start
- Confirm the failing route and collect sample request ids and timestamps (trace id)
- Check change window: recent kernel updates, model rollouts, infra changes, driver/OS updates

Tools used
- perf-trace: lightweight tracing agent that collects kernel timings (host + device), cudnn and cutlass timings
- rt-bench: runtime micro-benchmark harness (sequence length sweep, batch sweep)
- heap-snap: GPU/host memory snapshot tool
- flamegraph: CPU-side flamegraph generator
- prometheus + grafana dashboards for tail latency, queue length, batch size distribution

Profiling steps (ordered)
1) Reproduce in staging using same model version, kernel set, and sequence length distribution.
2) Run rt-bench sweep: sequences [8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256] x batch sizes [1, 4, 8, 16, 32]. Collect per-kernel latency and memory usage.
3) Collect perf-trace during a representative production window (30-60s).
4) Generate flamegraphs for CPU-side contention and record CUDA kernel occupancy and SM utilization.
5) Compare to baseline traces from last known-good release (artifact location: s3://redwood-runtime/prof-artifacts/{release}/).
6) If latency regressed: check for slow kernels, increased memory copies, kernel launches, or queueing at batcher.
7) Open a performance incident and tag owners (see Runbooks). Attach traces and rt-bench CSVs.

Artifacts to collect
- perf-trace tarball (host + device)
- rt-bench CSVs and JSON summary
- heap-snap output (GPU memory MAPPED/ALLOC metrics)
- Representative request payloads
- Prometheus timeseries for 1h before and after incident (latency p50/p95/p99, queue length, batch size)

Benchmarking suite (what to run for validation)

Bench types:
- Microbench: single-op and kernel latency profiling (used by kernel developers)
- Model microbench: single-model single-GPU steady-state throughput and latency sweep (rt-bench)
- System bench: multi-tenant packing, autoscaler stress, end-to-end API latency under synthetic load (k6 + workload generator)
- Regression harness: long-running periodic runs that compare current release vs baseline (nightly and pre-release)

Example test matrix (recommended):
- Models: tiny-llama-7B, llama-70B, rwx-chat-13B, rwx-code-16B
- Sequence lengths: 8, 32, 128, 512
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 8, 16, 64
- Dtypes: fp16, int8, 4bit

Sample configuration YAML (rt-bench)

# rt-bench config example
model: rwx-chat-13B
workload:
  sequences: [8, 32, 128, 512]
  batch_sizes: [1,4,8,16]
  samples_per_point: 100
kernels: [auto]
hardware: {gpu_type: a100-80gb, replicas: 1}

Interpreting results
- Primary metrics: tokens/sec, p50 latency, p99 latency, memory high-water mark, kernel occupancy
- Look for knee points: sequence lengths or batch sizes where latency jumps sharply
- Compare fp16 vs int8: note quality regressions tracked in model onboarding; if quality delta > threshold, mark kernel as not recommended for interactive routes

Release notes (latest stable runtime)

Version: 2027.08.01
- Kernel updates: added fused-attention-3 kernel (improves seq<=64 latency by 18% on A100)
- Scheduling: introduced adaptive-wait-window policy to reduce p99 for interactive routes by 12%
- KV cache: shard rebalancer improvements reduced cache-stall incidents by 45%
- Stability: fixed a memory leak in int8 dequantizer path that caused OOM after heavy sustained throughput
- Known regressions: on older Ampere drivers (<470.xx) fused-attention-3 falls back to slower code path; see Known issues below

Rollout notes:
- Canary rollout to 5% of traffic on 2027-07-15; full rollout completed 2027-08-01 following A/B validation
- Teams to validate: applied-ml-and-evals (quality checks), eng-sre (SLO telemetry), eng-serving-runtime (perf validation)

Known issues and mitigations

1) Fused-attention-3 fallback on older drivers
- Symptom: higher latency on A100 (drivers < 470.xx) when fused kernel is present
- Mitigation: pin driver OR force kernel to fallback to fused-attention-2 via runtime flag: --kernel-prefer=fused-attention-2
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime (Lucas Becker)

2) Intermittent KV cache shard hot-spotting
- Symptom: single shard receives disproportionate traffic causing local cache thrash and elevated latency
- Mitigation: trigger shard rebalancer (operational command: rws shard-rebalance --pool <pool-id>) and enable per-route rate-limiting; long term fix: fingerprint-based shard routing changes in next release
- Owner: eng-infra (Priya Nair)

3) Degraded p99 after enabling large batch packing across tenants
- Symptom: improved throughput but unexpected tail latency for interactive tenants
- Mitigation: constrain packing exposure for latency-tier routes (policy change) and enable adaptive-wait-window for those routes
- Owner: eng-platform (Mateo Rodrigues)

Runtime runbooks (quick actions for common incidents)

Incident: sudden p99 latency increase for interactive route
1) Confirm: check grafana dashboard (route p50/p99, queue length, batch size distribution).
2) Identify scope: global or pool-specific? Correlate with recent deploys.
3) Collect traces: perf-trace for 60s, rt-bench micro-run.
4) If queueing observed: scale up pool (rws pool-scale --pool <id> --replicas +2) and enable immediate fallback to slower but stable kernel (rws route-update --route <r> --kernel-fallback=true).
5) If kernel stalls: revert kernel rollout (rws release-rollback --release <release-id>).
6) Post-incident: open a postmortem, attach artifacts, and schedule kernel/packing policy follow-up.

Incident: OOM in executor process
1) Detect: node reports OOM, process restarts.
2) Quarantine: cordon node, move traffic away (rws pool-drain --node <node-id>).
3) Retrieve heap-snap and logs, check for known int8 dequantizer leak (matches stack trace?).
4) If leak found: revert to last stable release; if unknown, escalate to eng-serving-runtime oncall.

Operational commands quick reference
- rws pool-scale --pool <id> --replicas <n>  # scale replicas
- rws shard-rebalance --pool <id>               # rebalance KV shards
- rws release-rollback --release <id>         # rollback runtime release
- rws route-update --route <id> --kernel-prefer=<name>  # pin kernel for route

Telemetry and dashboards to check
- Runtime / Route SLO dashboard (p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, errors)
- Batcher metrics (avg wait, batch size distribution, dropped requests)
- Kernel inventory (per-kernel latency, occupancy, memory usage)
- KV cache metrics (hit rate, shard distribution, eviction rate)

Team wiki pointers and ownership

- eng-serving-runtime team wiki: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki (primary living index for experiments and internal HOWTOs)
- Kernel development guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling (kernel dev and testing checklist)
- Perf artifact storage: s3://redwood-runtime/prof-artifacts/{release}/
- Oncall rota: https://redwood-ops.example.com/oncall (eng-sre)

Appendix: example diagnostic checklist (copyable)

1) Route: ____________
2) Time window: ____________
3) Recent deploys: kernel_release=____, runtime_release=____, driver_version=____
4) Prometheus queries to copy:
- rate(requests_total[1m]) by (route)
- histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le,route))
5) Artifact locations to attach in ticket: perf-trace, rt-bench CSV, heap-snap, flamegraphs
